title: How a block of ice becomes a fridge (v5)
lines: Your fridge has never made anything cold. Not once.
A hundred years ago, a fridge was this: a wooden box, and a block of ice.
It worked brilliantly, for about two days.
Then the ice was a puddle, and the milk was yogurt.
Here's the thing: you can't make cold. You can only move heat out.
So swap the ice for a pipe, filled with a liquid that boils at minus twenty six.
Boiling soaks up heat, so it drinks the warmth right out of your food. This is the evaporator.
But now it's gas, and gas wants to escape.
So trap it, and crush it with a pump. This is the compressor.
Squeezed gas gets hot. Hot enough to burn your fingers.
Perfect. Snake it up the back, and the heat pours into your kitchen. This is the condenser.
That's why the back of your fridge feels warm.
As it cools, it turns back into liquid. But it's still squeezed tight.
So push it through a pipe thinner than spaghetti. The pressure drops, and it's ice cold again. This is the capillary tube.
Round and round it goes. Forever.
Which is a problem. Your lettuce is now a glass sculpture.
So add a sensor that cuts the pump when it's cold enough. This is the thermostat.
That's the click, and the hum that stops at night.
Add foam, a door seal, and a little light. Congratulations, you've built a fridge.
It never made cold. It just moves the heat from your milk, into your kitchen.
